newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Grief and anger at Belgian funeral of dead girl.
newsitem.headline: Grief and anger at Belgian funeral of dead girl.

text.p: Grief and anger swept Belgium, shaken by paedophile scandals, as 20,000 people attended the funeral on Saturday of a young girl found dead in the basement of a Brussels garage.

"My little Loubna. Our little Loubna, because you have become everyone's child. The child of a whole country," Nabela Beanaissa, 17, the dead girl's sister, said at the funeral. "Today pain unites us. Tomorrow I hope it will be love."
"Loubna, at last I can say goodbye to you. Goodbye in the name of all who love you," she said in an emotion-choked voice.

The body of Loubna Benaissa, aged nine when she disappeared in August 1992 while shopping for her mother, was discovered on Wednesday in a steel trunk in the basement of a garage in the Brussels suburb of Ixelles where she lived.
Patrick Derochette, a convicted child molester who worked at the garage, has been charged with the abduction, rape of a child under 10 and illegal imprisonment leading to death.

A representative of King Albert attended the funeral, as did members of the government, the parents of four other young girls who have been found dead since August and those of other children who are still missing.
"You are very strong and I embrace you very strongly," Marie-Noel Bouzet, the mother of Elizabeth Brichet who has been missing since December 1989, told Loubna's parents.

After the ceremony the small white coffin, draped in a black and gold prayer shawl, was taken to Brussels airport for a flight to the family's home town of Tangiers, Morocco, where Loubna will be buried there on Sunday.

Outside the Islamic Centre in central Brussels in the packed Cinquantenaire park, the atmosphere was equally emotional but without any of the incidents police had feared after a mini-riot by Moroccan youths in Ixelles on Thursday night.

"It is unbearable. We live in a rotten society...but we always have hope, hope that the world will change and become more caring," said Mohamed Drissi, tears streaming as he held the hand of his 4 1/2-year-old daughter.
"I came here for Loubna's brothers and sisters. The man who did that to Loubna should suffer the same fate. He should be shut up in a box," Inare, 10, told Reuters.
Nearby a small shrine to Loubna was covered with flowers, childrens' drawings and messages of sorrow and support.
Shock at the discovery of Loubna's body turned to anger at the evident bungling by Brussels police in the first investigation into her disappearance.

Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene admitted that mistakes had been made and steps would be taken. "It's clear that there is something wrong when discoveries are made now although all the elements are the same as four years ago," he said.
Asked on RTL-TVI television if racism had hindered the investigation, he said: "I hope that's not what we will discover - from time to time I fear it played a part."
He said the government would next week consider a proposal for longer minimum prison sentences for convicted paedophiles and closer surveillance after they were freed.
The discovery of Loubna's body brought to five the number of young girls found dead in Belgium since last August when another convicted paedophile, Marc Dutroux, was arrested.

Two young, sexually-abused girls were rescued from a dungeon in the basement of one of Dutroux' houses and the bodies of four girls were unearthed on two other properties either owned by or connected with him. Dutroux has been charged with murder.
A special parliamentary commission has increasingly focused on allegations of official protection for Dutroux since it began investigating the bungled police investigations five months ago.
The commission, which had been due to report on March 15, has new been given an extra month to pursue its inquiries.
